title: Learning Lesson 6: Multitasking is popular, but it doesn't work
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: This lesson introduces the first of Stephen Chew's learning "pitfalls" that Stuart teaches secondary students: multitasking and distractions greatly reduce learning. He works through concrete classroom examples of multitasking (switching browser tabs between subjects, watching YouTube while self-quizzing, texting during homework) and of common distractions (phones, video games, friends, siblings), pairing each with its solution — single-tasking and eliminating distractions, respectively. Stuart frames the needed disposition as "aggressive," using a personal anecdote about being told by a soccer coach to stop holding back and "go for it" as an analogy for how students should approach protecting their focus. He translates this into two concrete tactics: timed single-tasking blocks (25 minutes, phone away, one subject only) and finding a physical "hideout" free of the normal distractions of home, citing his own college library habit and a student who studies in a closet.
points: Stuart pairs each type of pitfall with an explicit, memorized solution: multitasking calls for single-tasking, and environmental distractions call for elimination, not willpower.

He uses a personal soccer-coaching anecdote ("be aggressive, get in there") as the through-line concept for the whole pitfall, reframing distraction-avoidance as an active, effortful stance rather than a passive hope.
The concrete tactic offered is a 25-minute single-tasking block: phone away, one subject only, until the timer ends.
The "hideout" strategy — a dedicated distraction-free physical space, even a closet — is offered as a practical fix for students whose home environments don't support focus by default.
quotes: Pitfall #1: Multitasking and distractions GREATLY reduce learning. Modern humans insanely underestimate the degree to which distractions harm their learning.
I want you to start thinking about learning a little more like an athlete, a little more like a gamer, a little more like someone who WANTS something, okay? Because listen — you DO want to learn.
And I remember one day my coach saying for the hundredth time, "Dave — be aggressive. Get in there. Go for it." And for whatever reason, that day it clicked.

When you're studying, just study. Set a timer for 25 minutes and for that 25 minutes you look at no other tabs, you chuck that phone right out the door, you put in some earbuds and you Just. Focus. On. Learning.
I've literally had students who study in the closet because it's the best hideout they can get in their living arrangement.
